title: Has King David's Palace in Jerusalem Been Found?
author: Israel Finkelstein; Ze'ev Herzog; Lily Singer-Avitz; David Ussishkin
publisher: Tel Aviv: Journal of the Institute of Archaeology of Tel Aviv University, vol. 34, no. 2
allowedUseNotes: Copyrighted peer-reviewed journal article. Project stores its own summary of the argument only; no reproduction of plans, photographs, or the article's text.
summary: A direct, named, Jerusalem-specific rebuttal of Eilat Mazar's 'Large Stone Structure' identification (mazar-2009-palace-of-king-david). The four authors argue that most of the massive walls Mazar presents as a single tenth-century BCE monumental building were in fact excavated and published decades earlier by Macalister and Duncan (1920s) and R.A.S. Kenyon, and belong to several different structures from several different periods, including Hellenistic-era construction -- not one coherent Iron Age I/IIA building. They dispute both the single-building reading and the proposed early tenth-century date, and by extension caution against reading the site's excavated remains as evidence for a developed administrative/monumental capital this early. This project cites this article as the named, Jerusalem-specific source for the 'modest fortified stronghold' pole of the tenth-century Jerusalem extent dispute (claim-jebusite-stronghold-form), alongside the already-cited finkelstein-silberman-2001 (which represents the same low-chronology pole at the level of the kingdom-scale debate generally, not with Jerusalem-specific excavation argument) -- this source supplies the missing site-specific citation the brief asked for.
